title: Aftermath and Blue Hour
premise: Ines Delacroix, a night librarian who has spent two decades perfecting the art of the unsaid sentence, learns that the childhood house where their brother Theo drowned is being auctioned by a cousin they haven't spoken to since the funeral. As Ines catalogues the house's contents for the estate sale — an inventory that becomes an inventory of everything never said about the night Theo died — they uncover evidence suggesting his death was not the accident the family agreed to call it. The auction becomes a deadline: once the house is sold and emptied, the last physical archive of the truth will be scattered. Ines must finally speak aloud what they witnessed at fourteen, forcing a reckoning with their mother's complicity and their own long silence, and in the blue hour before the sale closes, they choose testimony over inheritance, letting the house go but keeping, at last, the truth.
about_author: Jude Vasquez is the pen name of a former night-shift archivist who spent years cataloguing other people's unfinished letters. They write literary fiction about silence, family archives, and the ethics of remembering.

chapters.title: The Catalogue of Small Hours
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. We meet them shelving returns at 3 a.m., practicing sentences on index cards they never send. A certified letter arrives: the Delacroix house on Rue Sabine goes to auction in six weeks. Emotional beat: dread disguised as routine.

chapters.title: What the Water Kept
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, first flashback. The summer Theo drowned; fourteen-year-old Ines saw something at the pond's edge they have never named. Present-day Ines rereads the auction listing and feels the old sentence rising. Beat: the wound reopened.

chapters.title: A Cousin with Keys
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Cousin Marisol arrives unannounced, brisk and grieving in her own way, asking Ines to help inventory the house before the sale. Ines agrees for reasons they can't admit. Beat: reluctant alliance, mutual suspicion.

chapters.title: Inventory: Front Hall
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. First day in the house; dust, the coat rack, the phone that never rang for help that night. Ines catalogs objects with librarian precision as armor. Beat: grief arriving through objects rather than memory.

chapters.title: Mother, Declining to Comment
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Odile, Ines's mother, now in assisted living, sharp-tongued and evasive. When Ines mentions the auction, Odile says 'sell it all' too quickly. Beat: the first crack in the family's official story.

chapters.title: The Box Under the Stairs
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Behind loose paneling, Ines finds Theo's box: a diary, a pawn ticket, and a letter addressed to Ines, unfinished. The diary's last entries mention money and fear. Beat: discovery; the accident story begins to wobble.

chapters.title: Blue Hour Rules
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She reveals she has her own doubts — she found bank withdrawals in Aunt Odile's name the month Theo died. She and Ines agree to investigate quietly before the sale. Beat: alliance solidifies into conspiracy of two.

chapters.title: The Pawn Ticket
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Following the ticket to a shuttered shop and its elderly former owner, who remembers a man buying back a watch twice — a man who wasn't Theo. Beat: the past proving more populated than remembered.

chapters.title: Interlibrary Loan
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, at work. Using archival databases between patrons, Ines pulls old police reports and news clippings. The report contains an interview with Odile that contradicts her later statements. Beat: methodical hope, the librarian's justice.

chapters.title: Odile, Cornered by Morning
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Ines confronts her with the report; Odile deflects, then breaks slightly, admitting Theo owed dangerous people money. She denies knowing more. Beat: partial confession, deeper concealment.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She identifies the pawnshop man's associate: Renard, a debt collector still living nearby, old now, talkative at a bar. He hints he was at the pond that night. Beat: threat made flesh; stakes rise.

chapters.title: Chapter of Ash
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Someone breaks into the house overnight and burns the box's contents — except the unfinished letter, which Ines had taken home. Now someone else knows what they know. Beat: escalation, fear, resolve hardening.

chapters.title: Reading Theo's Handwriting
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines finally reads the letter: Theo wrote that if anything happened, it would look like an accident, and he named Ines as witness because Ines was always watching. Beat: devastating intimacy; the dead brother speaking at last.

chapters.title: What Ines Saw, Said to No One
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, full flashback chapter. The complete scene at the pond: Renard confronting Theo, the struggle, Ines hidden in the reeds, Odile's car passing without stopping. Beat: the novel's buried heart, spoken finally on the page.

chapters.title: Mother, Out Loud
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Ines reads Theo's letter aloud to her. Odile confesses she knew Renard threatened Theo and chose the mortgage over the son. Beat: climax of the familial arc; no absolution offered or granted.

chapters.title: Renard at the Auction Preview
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Renard appears at the preview event, smooth and menacing, warning them off. Marisol records him; he notices. Beat: open confrontation, danger now public.

chapters.title: The Librarian's Testimony
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines files a formal statement reopening the case, using the archived records, the letter, and their own eyewitness account — justice pursued through documents and voice, not violence. Beat: courage; the theme of speech fulfilled.

chapters.title: Sale Day
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs braided. Bidders move through the house while detectives interview Renard outside. Ines walks each room saying goodbye aloud, object by object. Beat: climax converging with elegy.

chapters.title: Lot 47: The Pond Key
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Among the lots, a small key Theo kept — opening a boathouse locker containing the watch and Renard's dropped lighter from that night. Physical proof, found too late for the case but not for the family. Beat: bittersweet vindication.

chapters.title: Odile's Blue Hour
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. On the empty porch at dawn, mother and child sit together without forgiveness, but with acknowledgment. Odile asks what Ines will do now. Beat: quiet aftermath; inheritance refused, memory kept.

chapters.title: Shelving Returns
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Back at the library, Ines donates Theo's diary to the city archive, publicly accessible — memory made common property. They write and finally mail one of the index-card sentences. Beat: release.

chapters.title: Aftermath and Blue Hour
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, coda. One year later: the case closed, Renard charged, the house occupied by a young family whose lights burn late. At the pond in the blue hour, Ines speaks Theo's name out loud, easily, for the first time. Beat: peace earned through speech.
